utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and outside the courtroom who are listening to these procedures. Due to a technical problem we have a delayed start today. I hope the system is now working well. As this is the beginning of the Defence case, I would kindly ask The Registrar to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Zdravko Tolimir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, are you receiving the translation, the interpretation in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. I am receiving interpretation in a language I understand; that is to say, the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would kindly ask for appearances because it's the beginning, commencement of the Prosecution case. The Prosecution first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon to General Tolimir, Mr. Gajic, everyone. My name is Kweku Vanderpuye. I am here today with Peter McCloskey, Senior Trial Attorney, and Ms. Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, and for Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May there be peace in this house for all those present, and may God's will be done in these proceedings as well as today, and may the outcome be as God wishes and not as I wish. I hope we will all benefit from these proceedings. The Defence is represented by Mr. Gajic, myself, as well as other team members who are not present in the courtroom, such as Mr. Todrovski and Stefanovic - thank you - as well as Kojnovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. This Pre-Defence Conference is being held pursuant to Rule 73 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of our Tribunal. The Chamber notes that the Defence's 65 ter list of witnesses and exhibits was filed in English on the 5th of December, 2011. The Defence notified the Chamber and the Prosecution of an intention to call a total of four witnesses; three fact witnesses, and one expert witness. All of these witnesses are proposed to be called viva voce. None of them have protected measures. The estimate of the total time to be used during examination-in-chief of these witnesses is 36 hours. Pursuant to Rule 73 ter, the Chamber may call upon the Defence to reduce the number of witnesses and shorten the estimated length for examination-in-chief for some of the witnesses. The Chamber sees no need to use its discretion to do either. The Defence is hereby granted leave to call the four proposes witnesses and use the estimated 36 hours. The Chamber wishes to remind both parties that the revised order concerning guidelines on the presentation of evidence and conduct of the parties during trial, issued on the 4th of February, 2011, applies equally to the Defence case as it did to the Prosecution case. I turn now to pending motions. The Chamber is currently seized of three motions, since some decisions were filed last week and this morning. The Defence has submitted two motions for admission of documents from the bar table filed in English on the 7th of December, 2011. Responses were filed by the Prosecution on the 21st of December. The decisions on these motions will be issued in due course. The Prosecution's motion to admit one document from the bar table, pursuant to the testimony of Ramiz Dumanjic filed on the 22nd of December, 2011, was provided to the accused in B/C/S on Monday, the 16th January, 2012. A response by the Defence, if any, is due on Monday, the 30th of January. I turn now to other pending matters. Duplicate exhibit issues. The parties were informed by an e-mail from the Court officer on the 17th of January that there were several duplicate exhibits in evidence. The parties have agreed via a Defence e-mail on the 18th of January on which duplicates should be removed. The Chamber has considered these information and hereby orders the Registry to make the necessary changes as agreed by the parties to remove the duplicates and file a memo on the record detail these corrections. I will now deal with one document in the custody of the Registry, but we have first to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, as usual, this is the right moment to raise any matters you wish to raise to health problems or detention matters, if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. No issues to raise concerning my health situation, as I do not use any medication; hence, I have no requests. And other than that, there are no problems to mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Are there any other matters to be discussed or raised during the Pre-Defence Conference? Nobody wants to have the floor. In that case, this concludes the Pre-Defence Conference. Since we had a delayed start today, I think there is no need for any break. I take it that there will be no opening statement so that we should immediately commence with the evidence of the first Defence witness. He should be brought into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. As you will certainly know, first the Defence and then the Prosecution has the opportunity to put questions to you. Mr. Tolimir will now commence his examination-in-chief and has the floor. Please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to greet Mr. Kralj and thank him for coming here to testify. I wish him a pleasant stay in The Hague and may he provided with all he needs by God in the future life. For the transcript, Witness, I'd like to ask you to tell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: My name is Slavko Kralj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, in brief terms, something about your military education, military background.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I completed, firstly, a school for non-commissioned officers in armoured units in Banja Luka in 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Following that, after five years, I passed the exam to achieve the rank of lieutenant of armoured units and was consequently promoted to officer rank of the then JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Next, I completed a professional officer school for staff duties, followed by a course for battalion commanders. Then, I had an exam to be assigned to the rank of major. Next, I completed an English language course in Belgrade which lasted for a year. I completed a preparatory course for members and participants of peacekeeping missions. I also underwent a course in diplomacy and a course for military attaches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I intervene for a moment. I just want -- like to know when this happened. When? Because you told us quite a lot about your career but not about the time. Could you tell us when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My exam to be promoted to the rank of major took place five years later, after 1967.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And when did you take part in this training about peacekeeping missions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once I completed the English language course, it was between February 1989 and February 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In the previous answer, the witness referred to the rank of "second lieutenant" rather than "major."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kralj. Since you mentioned you attended a course in 1989 and 1990, can you tell us something about your career after 1989?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Between February 1989 and February 1990, I was a member of the UN in the UNIMOG peacekeeping operation in Iran.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you only on that mission or some others as well?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: During that period of time, it was the only mission, following which I returned to my home unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what were your duties in the UN peacekeeping mission after 1990?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: As part of the UN mission, I was one of the 12 JNA members who were there alongside other members stationed in Iran. The task was to monitor the implementation of an agreement signed between Iraq and Iran along their 1.200 kilometre border. It was a multi-ethnic mission, comprising members of other armed forces, from a number of countries who were accredited by their hosts in order to take part in the mission. I was an observer along the border, and we were in charge of monitoring the implementation of a peace agreement and the truce that was in place in keeping with relevant UN resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kralj. Can you tell us something about your career once the mission with the UN was over?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Upon completion of the UN mission, I returned to my home unit, which is the training centre for armoured units in Banja Luka. My duty there was that of desk officer in charge of finance in the curriculum department.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: After that, I was seconded in October 1991 to the Knin Corps, where I spent around four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell the Chamber whether in that territory, which saw combat in the former SFRY in Croatia or elsewhere, you met any of your former colleagues from the UN mission?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: While I was in Knin during the period I specified, I came across a Swedish major who wore plain civilian white clothes as part of the European Community mission. We met at a number of meetings in the village of Pakovo Selo. That was the first person I met. I met another major subsequently, who was part of UNPROFOR. His unit was stationed in Croatia in Slavonia. I even recall his name, Raul Costa [phoen], from Argentina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber whether you exchanged your experiences and impressions of the Iran and Yugoslavia peacekeeping missions, and did you discuss your points of view given the different roles you assumed at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: The Swedish major whom I met in Pakovo Selo, while I was in Knin, pretended not to know me. He never returned to any negotiations in Pakovo Selo following that. In Gradiska, I met Raul Kosta, the Argentinian major. He commanded a communications battalion of UNPROFOR in Daruvar. It was a warm encounter. Following a number of dangerous joint patrols in Iran, it was exiting to run into an old mate from the UN, and it happened in a friendly way. I was surprised by something, though. Major Kosta took off his blue UN beret and literally told me this: Slavko, this is not a neutral UN mission such as the one we were participants of in Iran. This mission is here with the excuse of protecting the Serbs in the area; whereas its true goals are quite different. If these people are not helped they will have to go, whether they want it or not. And they are very scared. Just in case, you should have my address, my telephone number. And if you are ever in need of assistance anywhere in the world as a refugee, I will help you. His service lasted for about half a year, and I did not manage to see him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I thank the interpreters. Tell us if the population of Daruvar who are of Serb ethnicity remained in that area under the protection of the UN members, one of whom was this man Raul? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: In the general area of Daruvar, Okucani, Gradiska, no one Serb stayed. There was a military campaign and they were all driven out of the area across the river Sava.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, your colleague said that he was on a neutral mission in Iraq. What were the differences between that mission and the mission of the UN in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina? What are your impression and your opinion, based on your experience?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Let me first say that I am proud -- or, rather, that I was proud to have the opportunity to meet anybody in a UN uniform again, because I considered any such person as a member of my wider family. I was very disappointed by the role of the UN in Croatia, especially disappointed by the military monitors who, in accordance with the agreement on the withdrawal of weapons and control, engaged more in reconnaissance than in the mission assigned to them. Let me immediately add that the monitors were not accredited in the Republika Srpska, but there was an agreement that they were to be allowed to control the positions of deployment of some kinds of weapons that had been withdrawn from Slavonia to the south of the river Sava. As a liaison officer, with other officers who were in Slavonia, I sensed that the officers who -- that the officers on the other side were partial, that they had side with Croatia. In other words, they were not neutral and they acted more for the benefit of the Croats than they -- more than reporting on the events on the ground. I was taught when I was to become a UN monitor that I was supposed to be the eyes and the ears of the Secretary-General who, based on information received from me, should be in a position to take the right decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us more about your experience with the attitude of the UNPROFOR toward the Army of Republika Srpska and the other warring parties in the areas relevant for this trial, such as Srebrenica, Zepa, and others. Did you notice any differences there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: There was a huge difference. My mission in Iran was an unarmed monitoring mission. The only weapons we had were UN emblems and the UN flag; that is, the officers from various countries who were monitors there didn't carry any weapons. UNPROFOR had a different mandate. UNPROFOR was an army with fully armed units, with materiel and technical equipment. And they acted from the position of power. I never understood a rule they cherished; namely, shoot [Realtime transcript read in error "should the"] first and ask questions later. In subsequent conversations with UNPROFOR members, I came to understand that the members of the VRS were depicted to them in a very different way. Many of them didn't even believe me that I had been a UN mission member until I spoke to them in English and explained some procedures of ours. Later on they showed more respect. They advocated the thesis of freedom of movement, that they had the right to go wherever they wanted in whichever way they chose, although that was not their mandate. The original mandate was for them to be stationed in protected zones such as Gorazde, Srebrenica, Zepa, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now please tell the Trial Chamber, as an UN members --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: As an UN member --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- in 1989 and 1990, and a member of the VRS later, what were the differences in the use of UN forces for the prevention of conflicts and improving the relations between the warring parties? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: We had a clear mandate from the UN in Iran; whereas, here the first thing to do was to make peace, because without peace there can be no other activities. If the warring parties fail to agree on a cease-fire, any activities can be hazardous for the UNPROFOR itself, so the first thing to do was to make peace between the warring parties under the auspices of the UNPROFOR command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your first duty when the war began in Croatia? You mentioned the Knin Corps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I was recognised by Colonel Mesud Hasotic [Realtime transcript read in error "Mishud Hasodic"] of the Knin Corps who was chief of morale and legal affairs at the Knin Corps. He asked me, Do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I may interrupt you for a moment, sorry for that. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 12 of the transcript, in line 13, the name was incorrectly recorded. It should be "Mesud Hasotic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hasotic. This is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this correction. Please go ahead with your answer. Sorry. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Mesud Hasotic asked me if I spoke English. I smiled and answered, Yes, why? He replied, Tomorrow, the corps commander, General Vukovic, is receiving the ambassadors of the European Community, and I have a big problem. The interpreter who was supposed to attend the meeting suddenly had to leave for some private reasons. Can you interpret simultaneously from English into our language and back? Of course I asked him to give me some more detailed information, what they wanted to discuss at that meeting, Colonel Hasotic trusted me, and on the follow day I interpreted at that meeting. The participants of the meeting were the corps commander, General Vukovic; Colonel Hasotic; and Colonel Tolimir, which was his rank at the time, and that was the first time I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you have mentioned me, and I stand accused here, could you please specify the exact date and what those talks what the ambassadors of the European Community were about so that the Trial Chamber gets a complete picture?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: General, sir, that happened on the day following my arrival in Knin. The month was October and the year 1991. At the meeting, they discussed the military political situation in the region. The two ambassadors, and I remember that one of them was Italian and the other Belgian, they represented the European Community and they were dressed in white. They were stationed in Split. They had a number of questions about the military political situation, the situation in that part of the territory. And let me add that the corps at that time had JNA insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you remember, tell us where the other units of UNPROFOR or the forces' representatives of the UN were stationed during the war in Croatia? In which territories, in which towns, if you can remember? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: UNPROFOR units were stationed in Knin, Daruvar, and in Slavonia. I returned from Knin after four months, and I rejoined the 1st Krajina Corps, and I had contacts with the personnel in Slavonia and in the wider surrounding of Okucani.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there representatives of the UN in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war in Croatia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: The first representatives came to the Republic of Croatia. I had the opportunity and the pleasure, I may say, to witness the arrival of the forward detachment of the Canadian Reconnaissance Battalion. I was in Gradiska at the time, pursuant to the approval of the Main Staff commander. And there was also an approval given over the phone from Geneva by President Karadzic, that UNPROFOR units should be allowed to enter the territory of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the status or the position of UNPROFOR members in Bosnia during the war in Croatia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Officially, those were two missions. However, logistics and supply went through Croatia because there was a base there already, the UNPROFOR had developed infrastructure already, and they used Zagreb airport for supply. There was also a UNHCR base there. They also sported UN insignia. Small convoys travelled from Slavonia through Banja Luka to territories controlled by Muslims or Croats rather frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be useful later once we start discussing other matters, I mean the movement of these convoys. But let us finish with the following: What was your duty during the war in Croatia, and later on as a member of the VRS? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: In the Knin Corps, following the meeting organised by the corps commander, he ordered that I be assigned to Hasotic's department as interpreter, as there was a lot of need for translation and interpretation and there was no one else in the corps who could speak English. I remained in that position for about four months, as it was a secondment. After the four months, I was replaced and I returned to assume the duties of communications officer in the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka in the civilian affairs sector. I performed the same duties until the 3rd of November, 1994, when I was seconded again to the Main Staff of the VRS. There, I was appointed to act as interpreter until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what were your duties in the civilian affairs sector in the 1st Krajina Corps, and what were your duties in the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: In the civilian sector of the 1st Krajina Corps I was an interpreter and a liaison officer. As the liaison officer, I was in contact with UNPROFOR representatives as well as military observers who came from Slavonia to control the territory. I took part in receiving, escorting, and monitoring UNHCR and UNPROFOR convoys through RS territory, from Gradiska via Banja Luka, Jajce, and on to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What year were you seconded from Banja Luka to the Main Staff of the VRS, and what were your duties there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: The secondment took place on the 3rd of November, 1994. Upon arrival in the Main Staff, I received an additional duty, in addition to being interpreter, who was in charge of liaisoning with UNPROFOR and international organisations as the civilian affairs sector. I was also supposed to act as deputy chief of sector, Colonel Djurdjic [Realtime transcript read in error "Djuric"], Milos Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you were also deputy chief of sector, can you tell us whether you were privy to Mr. Djurdjic's affairs, to his tasks?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: With time I became acquainted with all administrative matters that Mr. Djurdjic was in charge of in the Main Staff, such as UNPROFOR co-operation as well as co-operation with the humanitarian administrations. He we focussed particularly on the administrative part. I need to say that he was the only person in that sector when I arrived. I could act in his stead in case of his absence, be it because he was on regular or sick leave. I was completely familiar with the procedure, although it took some time for me to be completely acquainted with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Just for the sake of the record, could you please repeat the name of Colonel Djurdjic, to have it clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Milos Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I heard "Djurdjic" instead of "Djuric." Could that be corrected, please. Not "Djurdic" but "Djurdjic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, this is not precise. I said not "Djuric" but "Djurdjic." Could that be corrected, please. The name is Djurdjic. I think in line 21, at the end it is correct, but it should not be recorded as "not Djurdic." We will not manage that, I am afraid. So please continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what was Mr. Djurdjic's position? And his sector for civilian affairs, did it exchange information with the security and intelligence sector of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic's sector, in terms of organisational structure, was directly under the Main Staff commander. The tasks of the sector were co-operation with UNPROFOR as well as co-operation with international humanitarian organisations and other civilian organisations. Mr. Djurdjic was in charge of all that. It had nothing to do with the security and intelligence sector. There was no direct connection in terms of line of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Previously, you mentioned the agreement on cessation of hostilities and freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we then see P101, which is the agreement itself. Sorry, it is P1011, dated the 31st of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we had a delayed start today. Therefore, I would propose that we have our first break now, resume at 4.30, then sit for one hour again, and then again a break so that our -- for three hours hearing would be from 3.00 to 4.00, from 4.30 to 5.30, and from 6.00 to 7.00. If you agree with that, then you should continue with this document after the break. We have our first break now, sir, and we will resume at half past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to make one correction of the transcript. On page 11, line 12, it should read, I quote: "I never understood a rule they cherished; namely, shoot first and ask questions later." Mr. Tolimir, please continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to show Exhibit P1011 in e-court. This is the agreement on a general cessation of hostilities of the 31st of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1994, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we do have the agreement. We see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the text of the agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at paragraph 2 where it states, I quote: "The cessation of hostilities will be supervised and monitored by UNPROFOR through the establishment of joint commissions. A central joint commission shall be established under the chairmanship of UNPROFOR, with initial meetings at the Sarajevo airport, and regional joint commissions shall also be established in permanent session as needed and as determined by the central joint commission." My question is: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber whether you know whether the central and regional joint commissions were actually formed on the territory of the warring parties? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: A central joint commission was formed, as well as a regional joint commission on the territory of the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you remember, can you tell us who were the members of this central joint commission from the Army of Republika Srpska and from the other parties to the conflict? Are you able to tell us who the members of that central joint commission were? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: At the beginning, for a time, General Gvero was a member of the central joint commission, as well as General Tolimir. Sometimes I also took part in these joint commissions as an interpreter. From the other side, there were also representatives by the Muslims and the Croats. I cannot recall their names right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to explain, briefly, what this central joint commission actually was, what it means? What did it comprise of? What were all the parties that were in it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: The central joint commission was chaired by the UNPROFOR, and it also included the parties to the conflict, representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska and representatives of the Croatian and the Muslim ones, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at paragraph 5 of this agreement, please, the paragraph that we can see on the screen, which states, I quote: "Full freedom of movement with appropriate procedures shall exist for UNPROFOR and other official international agencies, in particular UNHCR, in order to implement this agreement, to monitor human rights, and to deliver humanitarian aid, including medical supplies and evacuations. The parties commit themselves to full respect for the security and safety of UNPROFOR members and related personnel. UNPROFOR shall continue to prevent any abuse of freedom of movement by its personnel or convoys which might be of military benefit to either party." My question is: This provision that we've just read in paragraph 5 refers to two things; first of all, it talks about freedom of movement and it also talks about preventing any abuse of freedom of movement. Are you able to tell us if you had any knowledge about the abuse of or misuse of the UNPROFOR convoy and the humanitarian aid convoys, since that is something that is noted in this paragraph as one of the obligations of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: When the UNPROFOR was moving or the UNHCR, there were cases, first of all, when video equipment was carried, especially cameras, which were used to film the territory through which the convoy was passing. As a rule, the equipment was not announced previously, pursuant to procedures that were already agreed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you talk here about this equipment being used by convoys and UNPROFOR in order to gather data about one of the sides, do you know whether UNPROFOR took measures to prevent such activities, as it was duty-bound to do according to what it states here, any abuses by its members or humanitarian organisation personnel, as they were passing? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR would give explanations how the equipment was allegedly being used as personal equipment by individuals. They didn't take this seriously and did not prevent this. They allowed this policy to continue until instructions were received at the check-points to confiscate this equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since these misuses were repeated in a number of convoys until confiscation of equipment was introduced, were there any requests by the UNPROFOR staff regarding freedom of movement and requests not to hinder their activities in relation to the parties? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: UNPROFOR tried, in all possible ways, to enjoy full freedom of movement which to me, as a soldier and a former UN member, meant that this was just another name for spy work or the intelligence service which actually was demonstrated in quite few instances. Freedom of movement in this case indicates freedom of movement along pre-approved routes and providing security by the Army of Republika Srpska. The UNPROFOR did not have a mandate to be on the territory of Republika Srpska but to be in safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, are you aware if there was a particular procedure that was established to secure this freedom of movement that we talked about earlier? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Procedures were agreed for the movement of UNPROFOR during meetings of the central joint commission. This included convoys as well as individuals. In order to move around in the territory of Republika Srpska at all, UNPROFOR, through certain means of communication, was supposed to notify about the movement of convoys or UNPROFOR vehicles; for example, it was supposed to announce a convoy 48 hours in advance, and individual UNPROFOR vehicles were to be announced 24 hours in advance. Medical evacuations were urgent and as needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now look at D250. Can we look at D250 in e-court now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a report by Zdravko Tolimir on a meeting of the central joint commission, which was held on the 4th of January, 1995. The date on the actual report is the 5th of January, 1995. Thank you. You see the document in front of you. Can we now look at paragraph 5, please. This is on the second page. We can see paragraph 5 which states: "UNPROFOR will prepare a draft agreement on 'complete freedom of movement,' which will be agreed bilaterally with the parties." My question is: Do you know whether the Serbian side entered into an agreement with UNPROFOR pursuant to a draft prepared by them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: The Serbian side signed an agreement on freedom of movement which implied appropriate procedures which were referred to in the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the other parties also sign the agreement, and do you know if they adhered to the agreement that they signed, if they did sign it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: As far as I know, the other side - I am thinking of the Muslim Croat side - never signed the freedom of movement agreement, and if they didn't sign it then they couldn't have adhered to it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you remember, are you able to tell us briefly why they didn't want to sign the agreement, if you know this through the work of the central joint commission? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: First of all, UNPROFOR was stationed on their territory. They believed that they shouldn't sign it, and they even offered - and it surprised me, the statement by a certain Mr. Muratovic - that the airport which at that time was under our control, they leased out to UNPROFOR in return for money. I cannot state whether this was accurate or not, but all of these things indicate that, according to my knowledge, the UNPROFOR and the Muslim and the Croat side agreed amongst themselves what was supposed to be done before the central joint commission convened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D77, next. The title is: "The Principles of the Freedom of Movement." [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we also see the second page of this document. We be see the signatures. On the left-hand side we have General Brinkman on behalf of UNPROFOR. On the right-hand side we have Major-General Zdravko Tolimir, as a representative of the VRS. Could we now go back to page 1, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who or what convoys did these principles apply to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: This agreement pertained to UNPROFOR convoys, as well as to individual movements of the UN military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. To your knowledge, was this agreement honoured in practice by the signatories; that is to say, UNPROFOR and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: The agreement was honoured in full by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain the procedure of approval for UNPROFOR convoys or, rather, what was the procedure like in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: In keeping with the agreement on the principles for freedom of movement, UNPROFOR forwarded notifications of convoys. There was an UNPROFOR office in the territory of the RS at Pale. They had a telefax which was used to forward notifications of convoy movements to Colonel Djurdjic's office. There was a telefax machine on the other end which used a civilian number. It was on around the clock; in other words, messages could be sent and received automatically, nonstop. Originally, notifications were sent in both English and in translation into Serbian. Due to poor communication links or illegible fax messages, it happened that the notifications had to be cross-referenced or compared, since, under the agreement, the English text had precedence. Once the office was in receipt of an accurate notification of UNPROFOR movement, it was put in the mail, sent to the commander for his attention. The commander, as part of his regular daily reading of mail, reviewed the document, initialled it, and introduced remarks if he deemed it necessary. Through operational channels, the document was then returned to Colonel Djurdjic's office. What followed was a document which was used to notify UNPROFOR -- or, rather, its office at Pale, that there were no specific issues concerning the requested movements of convoys or observers. Another such document was sent to the unit in charge of monitoring the movement of the convoy in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether this central joint commission had anything to do with these convoy movements?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: The central joint commission set up procedure, the procedure that had to be respected by Colonel Djurdjic and others on the part of the VRS involved in such movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Concerning these UNPROFOR convoy notifications, was there an arrangement or an agreement reached at the level of the central joint commission?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: It was the starting point. The arrangement at the level of the CJC was the starting point of the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you say it was the starting point, did your sector for civilian affairs receive information on the work of the central joint commission?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: We had the final document produced by the central joint commission; that is to say, we knew of the things that were supposed to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have D254.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting for it, can you tell us this: Were specific amounts and cargo discussed at the level of the central joint commission, as per individual convoys?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: There was discussion about the items which could be transported by trucks at the level of the central joint commission. Quantity was discussed as well, given the fact, in particular, that there was an embargo on the import of weapons and ammunition into Bosnia-Herzegovina. We had verified information that UNHCR and UNPROFOR convoys were being used to supply ammunition and even weapons, as well as fuel, to the enclaves or protected areas. If I may add, when I was still with the 1st Krajina Corps, one entire UNHCR convoy from Gradiska, once checked, returned to Zagreb airport without any explanation. There was a lot of effort invested in the convoy arriving, but once the checks and controls were set up at certain points along the route, the convoy turned back to Zagreb and never attempted to use the same route with the bills of lading they had at the time; although, I remember that it included food, flour, and other items.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now that you mention it, can you tell the Chamber why the convoy turned back of its own accord so that I wouldn't have to speculate?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: While I was the liaison officer of the 1st Krajina Corps, we checked documents and the drivers. We did not inspect the convoys in detail because this was a sealed cargo, followed by notifications and documents, and we still trusted them. However, once we began requesting that the cargo be inspected by way of random samples, and when I say that I mean that the personnel at the check-point would choose one or two trucks at random and use metal detectors to check the cargo, the convoy leader called his office in Zagreb and refused to submit to such an inspection. Since we were in a large parking area, he ordered that the convoy turn back, and they went back to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I called up a document which is now in front of you. It is dated the 12th of February, 1995, by the Main Staff. It was signed by General Tolimir. We'll see that later on. It was forwarded to all the commands of the VRS, as well as their -- as well as to the organs of the interior. It involved UNPROFOR movement in the territory of Republika Srpska and a certain procedure mentioned. I will read the first paragraph: "Through the regional joint commissions, UNPROFOR representatives are constantly bringing up the issue of greater freedom of movement for UNPROFOR across the front line with the aim of getting authorisation to cross the front line and move in the territory Republika Srpska on the lower regional levels while not having to notify the Main Staff of the VRS of all movements and not to having to wait for authorisation by the Main Staff of the VRS before doing so. "This is how UNPROFOR representatives wish to avoid complying with the obligation they undertook when they signed the obligations set out in the agreement on Principles of Freedom of Movement signed on 31 January 1995 by the Main Staff of the VRS (Major-General Zdravko Tolimir) and the UNPROFOR command for the former BH (General Brinkman). We hereby forward the entire text of the agreement." What followed is a number was procedures. Are you familiar with such UNPROFOR attempts as referred to in the first paragraph? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: I am familiar with these intentions of UNPROFOR for two reasons, one of them being the fact that Colonel Djurdjic informed me of that. He received relevant information and was in constant contact with the units that conducted checks at check-points. Also, the duty officer of the Main Staff, received reports from units about UNPROFOR activities. That was supplementary information that was included in such reports, but I paid special attention to it. Often times there were instances when UNPROFOR requested that military monitors for smaller convoys be led to pass. However, that was not covered by the agreement on the central joint commission, nor did they honour the -- the notice period, that is 24 or 48 hours in advance, without there being an urgent need for that. There were even attempts at bribing the personnel at the check-points with the fuel and other stuff for them to let them pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please explain, briefly, why UNPROFOR tried so hard to pass the check-points and cross the front line which was not in accordance with the agreements reached at the central joint commission and without a permission to move about in the territory of the RS?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: There was intelligence about what was going on and what the situation was like under UNPROFOR control. This intelligence shows that they also had -- also engaged in other activities; namely, supplying or informing the Muslim or Croatian side of what the VRS were doing. Specifically, the military observers needed some time to pass through a certain territory. They could observe military positions or carry or deliver something to the opposing side, for example, ammunition. And I am talking about extensive territories and unit movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were on a UN mission in Iraq, as you said, and you also took part in the war and carried out some duties that had to do with the UN and UNPROFOR, can you point out the differences with regard to the freedom of movement of UN forces in the RS as compared to the situation in Iraq or Iran where you were on mission? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: There was a huge difference. I was in Iranian territory as an observer, but we were unable to go anywhere, officially or not, without being escorted by some people that were called liaison officers. There was a check-point and you couldn't pass there to go to a sector without an escort, let alone to the demarcation line or any other place. You always needed their military escort and a liaison officer who, of course, spoke English. Here, UNPROFOR had a much greater freedom of movement. All that was required was a check at the point of entry and another at the point of exit from the territory in question. They also had to move along a certain route. It happened very rarely that they had an armed military escort, but they didn't want one, either, because they were armed themselves. Their military observers were armed; whereas, over there, the only weapons that we had were the UN insignia and the UN flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that they didn't want an armed escort. Did they have any kind of escort while moving through RS territory, armed or unarmed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: The UNHCR was escorted in the territory of the 1st Corps. They were escorted by the military police and sometimes, if necessary, by the civilian police. Since we are talking about a territory that stretches from Gradiska to Travnik, that is, it's rather extensive. That escort was to vouch, say, for the security of the convoy and make sure that it really reaches its destination. As a liaison officer, I had very unpleasant experiences. There were instances when the local population accused the VRS of nurturing them while their sons were dying on the battle-field. I am talking about convoys that were supposed to cross the demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw that agreement on the cessation of hostilities. I quoted from it. The UNPROFOR was duty-bound to sanction any misuse on the part of their members. Was the VRS in the position to do anything of the kind in the territory through which they moved?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: The VRS could step up the controls at the check-points. They could inspect their cargo, and they could compare the amount of cargo to some standards that apply to the unit -- to the respective unit in the field. There are some standard requirements for provisions of food or fuel or ammunition for units of various types.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us who it was in the VRS who checked UNPROFOR convoys to prevent a misuse?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: The first -- the first level was Colonel Djurdjic's office. He would study each notification, and in his absence I would do it, and check if it was in line with the provisions of the agreement reached by the central joint commission. Of course, it was impossible for everything to be agreed upon there. Then estimates were made whether the goods transported were something that UNPROFOR needed or, possibly, the population, or, in the worst case, military units; that is, the Muslim army in the enclave, such as Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When Djurdjic gave approval for the passage of a convoy which was announced to the Main Staff, did he do it arbitrarily or were there any criteria that Djurdjic had to honour in the process? In other words, did Djurdjic make a proposal which had to be approved by the commander? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: In the office, aggregate statistics were made about the quantities of the sensitive goods, such as fuel, ammunition, and suspicious materials. The data was collected at the check-points, and through a liaison officer or another person at the corps command, relayed to the operative component of the command and also to Colonel Djurdjic's office. Colonel Djurdjic was able to give information to the commander, how much of a certain type of goods entered any particular enclave in a period of time, especially Srebrenica, Zepa, or Gorazde, and he was in a position to suggest that the quantities received during a certain period were sufficient or insufficient. However, those quantities were invariably two or three times greater than what was necessary for the units that were there, although their standards were somewhat different from ours, but not that much. Colonel Djurdjic received notifications in due time, and he had time enough to visit our logistics organs who were in charge of feeding the army. He gained immediate knowledge of the standards of the -- applicable to food or fuel required per soldier or per unit in a certain period of time. Consequently, he was in a position to make a suggestion to the commander that certain quantities should be reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go to the last page of document D254, in paragraph 2. I read: "You need to send us a list of goods whose transport should be prohibited. You are to prepare this on the basis of past experience with fraudulent dealings and abuses by UNPROFOR. After your proposals have been reviewed, you will be given a list of goods whose transport is prohibited unless expressly approved by the Main Staff of the VRS and announced to you." Here is my question: Since you've just spoken about Djurdjic's detailed analysis of the requirements of the opposing side or UNPROFOR, can you tell us whether the Main Staff took care of -- or, rather, the Main Staff had a relevant knowledge of what could or could not be let pass to go to enemy territory? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Once we learned of the misuse of UNPROFOR and UNHCR convoys, more attention was being paid by the Main Staff to the cargo itself that was being transported by those convoys, particularly if it was assessed that the cargo in question was not something that was needed for UNPROFOR or the civilians in the enclaves, but, rather, the military forces there. Careful records were kept of what and how much cargo was transferred into the enclaves which should allow for a normal functioning of UNPROFOR. Weekly plans were drafted and agreed with UNPROFOR, and they were planned for a few weeks in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is time for a break, and with your leave, Mr. President, I will wait with my next question until later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a good proposal, indeed. We need the second break and we will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we look at 1D874 in e-court now, please. This is a memorandum to the Drina Corps command on the 29th of July, 1993. Can we please rotate the document. In the second paragraph, it states, I quote: "We have information that UNHCR officers engage in intelligence and reconnaissance activities which should be kept in mind during checks and other activities at your disposal."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is: In the 1st Corps, at the time did you receive similar memos and information, and did you receive information like that later at the Main Staff in relation to conduct by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: While I was in the 1st Krajina Corps, I did not receive the document, the complete document, but we would get excerpts from some data relating to misuses by UNPROFOR and the UNHCR. We were given guidelines to conduct special checks, at that time, of the UNHCR which was passing through the Gradiska territory towards the line of separation and towards the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you have information about intelligence activities conducted by UNHCR members during their passage to the enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Members of UNHCR and UNPROFOR sought, very often, ways, how to pass through the territory. There were instances when their officers were sent, and military observers, to carry out some reconnaissance activities, mostly recording and monitoring positions of the VRS that were registered earlier or noted earlier. This was supplied to the UNPROFOR command, and according to some data that I had at my disposal, this data was also made available specifically to those in Srebrenica, Muslim forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether that was one of the reasons to ban the movement of unannounced convoys and to prevent bringing in technical and other equipment which could be used for intelligence activities? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: That was the only and the main reason why something was not permitted. This applied to anything that could be used in intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED [Interpretation] Can we have this 1D874 admitted? I would like to tender that. And can we -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D325. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we now look at Exhibit D73. D73. Well, we can't see it yet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the document now. The title of the document is: "Movement by Convoys, Teams, and Individuals from UNPROFOR and Humanitarian Organisations." Can we now look at the last page of the document so that we could see who drafted it. Here is a name and surname written in the Latin alphabet in the Serbian. Could you please read that and tell us whether you know the person who wrote and drafted this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: It says clearly here "Kapetan," Captain Slavko Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you have read this, tell us, do you know who Captain Slavko Novakovic is, whose signature we see here, and can you tell us what was his post at the time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Captain Novakovic was in the logistics sector of the Drina Corps, and besides carrying out his regular duties he was also carrying out the job of liaison from the corps with the UNPROFOR and the UNHCR, and he also kept a record of the quantities and problems that he had with the UNHCR and UNPROFOR during their passage throughout the territory. He was also in charge of organising and overseeing the work of the check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 2, please. Paragraph with the title: "Behaviour and Abuse of Mandate by UNPROFOR and Humanitarian Organisations." This is marked C.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please look at the document. The first paragraph -- you can look at the whole document as well, I don't mind at all.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in a little bit on the paragraph at the top in the heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: You have now looked at the document. Did you receive these documents and was your sector aware of this information from subordinate units, such as this report by Captain Slavko Novakovic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: These reports were sent to Colonel Djurdjic's office. He reviewed them in detail, as needed. And if needed, he would even go to Captain Novakovic to clarify some details from certain documents with him in person. These were abuses that are referred to in the text below, which required a particular kind of action in the process of approving the passage of the convoys -- in the process of the passage of the convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware of information about abuses of humanitarian aid convoys in the Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde enclaves? Did your office have this information?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Our office received relevant information to the effect that certain quantities of assistance were being delivered to the army of the Muslims in Srebrenica. They didn't specify concrete quantities. And Colonel Djurdjic, since I was busy with other tasks, always used the opportunity to inform me about these cases. I didn't receive information as such. I received information from Colonel Djurdjic and he, in turn, received the appropriate information from the intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the last paragraph. Can we scroll the document up so that we could see the whole paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am going to read it. It's quite small type. I quote: "Understandably, most cases of attempted smuggling of goods were in the convoys for Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, which had the fewest possibilities for being provisioned apart from humanitarian aid. The following goods were those that were most smuggled: Video cameras, cameras, film, weapons, radio sets, satellite equipment and antennae, signaling apparatus, optical devices, night vision apparatus, motor oil, various parts for devices, anti-freeze, chemical manure, oxygen cylinders, flak jackets, helmets, sleeping bags." My question is: Is this equipment for the needs of the civilians or for the use of the army that is being referred to here in this paragraph, and can it be used for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: This equipment can be used both for civilian and military uses; however, a flak jacket can only be used by a soldier, and all UNPROFOR members had a sufficient number of flak jackets for their needs. Other equipment, especially for night recording, was of exceptional importance to the other side so that they could use infrared devices for night monitoring in the area under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska or to infiltrate their own special units. If they were equipped with this infrared equipment, the binoculars, they could, unhindered, from a certain distance, safely observe and gather data about what was being done in the territory that was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I stop you for one short moment. Sir, have you any idea when this document was written and sent to the recipient? Can you take that from the text or from somewhere else? Or do you recall this specific document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see a date in the heading. Generally speaking, I recall such reports as some of the reports which arrived from Novakovic were archived in Colonel Djurdjic's office. I can't say exactly which report this is, though, but they were similar in terms of content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please help me. Where do you find the date, as you said? You said, "We can see a date in the heading." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had in mind the time the document was drafted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you see the date? Shall we go back to the first page, or what is your proposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not see a precise date, but the document refers to 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the one, two, three -- fourth longer paragraph in the middle, it says -- it speaks about personnel who have been working at this task since August 1993. Do you see that? Is that correct? I am asking you because the document itself doesn't bear any specific date when it was drafted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It mentions the Drina Corps and a reserve captain thereof. In this case, it is Slavko Novakovic who was a reserve captain. He was assigned to monitor all UNPROFOR-related matters. This references to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the next -- and the last paragraph on this page, you will see a reference to August 1994; is that correct? Especially to instructions of August 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What would be your conclusion when this document was drafted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please bear with me, I'd like to read it more carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then I take you back to the first paragraph on this page. In the first paragraph, it says: "Convoys, teams, and individuals from UNPROFOR and others entered the Drina Corps zone of responsibility and moved about therein on a daily basis during 1994 using the following roads:" Can I take it that this must have been drafted sometimes in 1995 as it relates to the whole year of 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This seems to be a summary report of convoy movements in this period up to August 1994. Obviously the document was drafted on Djurdjic's request for a specific information and issues. It was in a collated summary form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Slavko, please tell us whether, save for the procedure reported here, was it also known in the Main Staff that the BH Army was also supplying itself by way of humanitarian aid convoys as well as UNPROFOR convoys?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: General, sir, this was one of the specify sources. The Main Staff had a number of other sources and possibilities at their disposal as well as other information about the use of UNHCR and UNPROFOR convoys in order to supply military assets and cargo that is not permitted to those in the enclaves. Bihac was another problematic area in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D458 next. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see it here. I will quote, briefly: "We forward an overview of the amounts of food, materiel, and technical equipment, as well as fuel, issued to the military units in our area in March 1995: Flour, 18 tonnes; beans, 6 tonnes; kitchen salt, 450 kilogrammes; sugar, 470 kilogrammes; edible oil, 1.2 tonnes; canned food, 9.900 pieces; powder milk, 750 kilogrammes. "We also draw your attention to the fact that the specified quantities were taken out of the contingent of humanitarian assistance which arrived in this area via UNHCR and it is our only source of supply." The document was drafted by Mr. Sulejman Hasanovic, who was chief of the defence secretariat in Srebrenica, and he forwarded this letter to the defence secretariat in Tuzla. Can you tell us what this data is all about and it comes from their source?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: This data, without a doubt, show that the Muslim army was supplied by way of UNHCR contingents delivered to Srebrenica, and we have the specific amounts for a specific period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can such quantities of food be used to feed the unit, as it was, in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: In addition to UNPROFOR within the protected area of Srebrenica, there were armed Muslim units which, to my -- well, first of all, to my knowledge that unit was supposed to have been demilitarised in the first place; however, they had standing units which received part - a significant part - of their supplies from the UNHCR. We can see they received oil -- well, we can't really see if it's engine oil or cooking oil, but we see some other items as well. In other words, this enabled the army in the enclave to provide food for themselves and even to store supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see that this refers to the 31st of March, 1995, and it is in reference to the register of donations to the Army of BiH. We can see that it arrived by way of convoys?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Since there is no translation available yet, it will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D458 shall be assigned Exhibit D326, marked for identification pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have just seen this document D325 about how the UNHCR, in March 1995, supplied the Army of BH. Could we next have D80 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, to avoid any complications with numbers, you just referred to document P325, but what we have seen was D326. So I misspoke. I meant "D325."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We have D80 in front of us. It is another document of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's Tuzla defence secretariat, or rather, department of that secretariat in the municipality of Srebrenica. The document is dated the 5th of June, 1995, two months following the previous document. Subject: Records of donations to the BH Army. It states: "We hereby submit a list of the quantities of food, materiel, and technical equipment and fuel issued to our military units in our area for the month of May 1995." We see that it refers to 25.900 kilogrammes of flour; 596 kilogrammes of sugar; 1.423 litres of cooking oil; 619 kilogrammes of salt; 5 tonnes of beans; 17.020 cold cuts; 100 kilogrammes of powder milk; 62 kilogrammes of juice; 7.780 tins of fish; 117 pieces of breaded fish; 480 kilogrammes of ground meat, et cetera. Signed by chief of the defence sector Professor Suljo Hasanovic. Towards the bottom, the penultimate line, we see the following: "We wish to note that the above quantities have been separated out of the humanitarian aid contingent which arrived in the area through the UNHCR, while some of the food was obtained by the Dutch Battalion." Did Colonel Djurdjic's office have information about an increase of food supplies carried by UNHCR convoys with an aim of supplying the BH Army? And we also see here that even UNPROFOR provided some of the supplies.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: We had information that the UNHCR convoys, and also the Dutch Battalion, partly supplied the Muslim army, especially in Srebrenica. To my mind, and I am well acquainted with the principles governing the work of the UN, it is conspicuous here that anything that bears the UN logo is somehow co-ordinated. Most probably the UNHCR transported larger quantities of flour, so it was them rather than UNPROFOR, and the same applies to any other goods because the observers, based on their estimates, would be able to see that the Dutch Battalion didn't need so much flour. It isn't stated here who transported the goods, it is only mentioned that both gave as much as they could spare. And I'm particularly referring to the Dutch Battalion here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see D197. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You can see a document of the Bosnia and Herzegovina embassy and the Republic of Croatia, more specifically its military economic mission in Zagreb. They sent a document to the Bihac office to the attention of the commander of the BH Army 5th Corps. All these items are about military assets, exclusively lethal assets; fuses, ammunition, grenades, large quantities of all these. And the last sentence reads: "Please provide confirmation of received MTS," which stands for materiel and technical equipment, "or problems concerning reception." And the following line identifies the UNHCR truck. It says that it's license plate number is 10379. It is signed by Hajrudin Osmanagic for the military attache. This document is from 1993 at which time you were in the zone of responsibility of the 1st Corps. Tell us first what this means, truck number UNHCR-10379? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: This number is the license plate on the truck, UNHCR plus a five-digit number. Such trucks passed through the zone of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps. They bore the same license plates. Trying to refresh my memory now. When the UNHCR convoy returned from the check-point at Gradiska, I am fully certain that it was at the time stated here. The difference may have been a few days earlier or later. The UNHCR convoy turned around when we wanted to inspect it thoroughly, especially when they saw that there were metal detectors available at the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During that period you are referring to, what about the convoys that were not to be thoroughly inspected? Could they transport military equipment that was declared as humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Yes, it was possible for them to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there other means of supply of military equipment such as the equipment stated here? Could such equipment pass through check-points in UNPROFOR vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: General, sir, at that time there was a no-fly zone over BH territory. There were also clashes between Croatian and Muslim forces. Let me add that the supply of Bihac went mostly from Croatia to that area, and they did not go through RS territory. I am talking about humanitarian aid. Probably, taking into consideration the opposites of supplying an army, there was intelligence and there were observed flights, illicit flights, to Tuzla airfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the enclaves Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, could they receive supplies through these convoys or were there other options available?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: There were other options.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Which other options do you know of that could be used to supply military units in the enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: There were also instances of smuggling. There were instances of dropping equipment from planes. I think those were C-135 planes. This plane was identified a couple of times based on the specific sound it produces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see document 65 ter 04911. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see it. This is a document of the Main Staff of the VRS. It's dated 9 January 1995, and addressed to the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo. It was signed by Chief of Staff, Lieutenant-General Manojlo Milovanovic. I don't think I need to read it. You can see it. What is this document about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: This is a document sent by the Main Staff to the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo. To be more precise, to the UNPROFOR office at Pale. And they forwarded it to their command in Sarajevo. The document is marked 06. These are the first two digits, which means that it was entered in the list of documents of the office of Colonel Djurdjic. Could we please zoom in on the letterhead? Could we scroll down? Here we see 18 activities of convoys, 18 crossings that were approved to go through the territory of the RS; for example, convoy number so-and-so, its route, and the time-frame, for example, 10 January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from travelling through RS territory and having the approval to cross the front line to go to BH Army controlled territory, that is an army that was at war with the VRS, and go into enclaves such as Sarajevo, Srebrenica, which means that they had to cross more than one front line; is that correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: Each convoy is different. The one going from Kiseljak to Srebrenica or Gorazde or Zepa had to cross two demarcation lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, who has the authority in an army to authorise a convoy to cross the front line from enemy-held territory to your own territory or in the opposite direction? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: For crossing from one side to the other, that kind of authority is only with the commander or with a person authorised expressly by him, personally by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "commander," do you mean the commander of the army or a lower-level commander? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ
utterances.text: General, sir, this is a document of the Main Staff. It's the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS who has that authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 16 of this document in the Serbian language. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I have a question for you. You said on page 46, lines 7 through 8: "The document was sent by the Main Staff to UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo. To be more precise, to the UNPROFOR office at Pale." This was what was recorded. Where did you take that from, that it was sent to Pale and not to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
